title: Claw Hammer — Driving and Pulling Nails
body: Hold the hammer near the end of the handle for driving power, and choke up near the head for control. To drive a nail: hold it near the tip, tap it in to stand it up, then move your fingers away and strike squarely. Let the hammer's weight do the work — a smooth swing beats muscling it. The claw's V-slot pulls nails: slide it under the head and lever back, placing a wood block under the head for leverage and to protect the surface. Wear safety glasses; a glancing blow can send a nail flying.
capabilities: Explain the two-stage nail driving method

title: Screwdriver — Turning Screws Without Stripping
body: Match the tip to the screw: Phillips, flathead, Torx, or Robertson — the wrong tip strips the head. Push firmly while turning so the tip stays seated; most stripping comes from too little downward pressure. Turn clockwise to drive in, counterclockwise to remove (righty-tighty, lefty-loosey). For tough screws, tap the screwdriver handle lightly with a mallet while turning to break corrosion loose. Magnetic tips hold small screws in awkward spots.

title: Hand Saw — Straight Cuts by Hand
body: Mark the cut line on both faces, then start the cut with short, light pull strokes to establish a kerf. Let the saw's teeth do the cutting — pushing hard bends the blade and wanders the cut. Keep your eye on the line, not the blade, and use long smooth strokes. Support the waste side of the board so it doesn't splinter as it breaks free. A sharp saw cuts fast with little pressure; if you are forcing it, the blade is dull.

title: Power Drill — Drilling and Driving
body: Choose the right bit and chuck it tight; a loose bit wobbles and snaps. For twist drilling, mark the spot with a center punch so the bit doesn't wander. Run the drill fast for small bits in soft material, slow for large bits in metal, and use cutting oil on steel. Back the bit out periodically to clear chips. When driving screws, set the clutch low and raise it until the screw seats without stripping.

title: Adjustable Wrench — Nuts and Bolts
body: Adjust the jaw to fit the nut snugly — a loose jaw rounds the corners off. Always pull the wrench toward you rather than pushing; if it slips you won't smash your knuckles. Position the wrench so the fixed jaw takes the load, with the handle pointing in the direction of the pull. Never extend the handle with a pipe (cheater bar) on a small wrench — it snaps the tool. For plumbing, a second wrench holds the pipe while the first turns the fitting.

title: Pliers — Gripping, Bending, Cutting
body: Slip-joint pliers adjust to two jaw openings for gripping different sizes. Needle-nose pliers reach into tight spaces and bend wire precisely. Lineman's pliers cut and twist wire and hammer lightly in a pinch. Grip near the pivot for maximum force, and keep fingers clear of the handles' pinch zone. Diagonal cutters are for cutting wire only — never use them on hardened nails or bolts.

title: Spirit Level — True Horizontal and Vertical
body: Place the level on the surface and center the bubble between the lines for true level. Flip the level end-for-end and check again — if the bubble reads the same, the level is accurate. Longer levels are more accurate over distance; a 4-foot level beats a torpedo level for hanging shelves. For vertical (plumb) work, use the vial marked for vertical orientation. Laser levels project a line across a whole room for tiling and trim work.

title: Tape Measure — Measuring Right the First Time
body: The hook at the tape's end slides slightly — that movement equals the hook's thickness, so inside and outside measurements both read true. For inside measurements, read the tape at the far wall and add the case length printed on the case. Burn an inch: start at the 1-inch mark instead of the hook end for precise work, then subtract one inch. Lock the blade before reading, and let it retract slowly to protect the hook. Measure twice, cut once.

title: Wood Chisel — Paring and Chopping
body: A sharp chisel is safe; a dull one needs force and slips. Pare with the bevel down for controlled slicing, bevel up for chopping into the cut. Always cut away from your body and keep both hands behind the cutting edge. Chop mortises in shallow passes, clearing waste between passes. Tap with a wooden mallet, never a steel hammer, which mushrooms the handle.

title: Sandpaper and Sanding — Smooth Finishes
body: Sandpaper grit numbers run backward: lower numbers are coarser. Work through the grits — 80 to 120 to 220 — never skipping more than one step, or coarse scratches remain. Always sand with the grain; sanding across it leaves visible scratches. A sanding block keeps the paper flat and prevents finger-shaped dips. Wipe off dust between grits so coarse particles don't contaminate the fine paper.

title: Utility Knife — Controlled Cutting
body: Extend the blade only as far as the cut needs — a long blade snaps and wanders. Score materials like drywall and cardboard with several light passes instead of one deep cut. Cut away from your body, on a stable surface, with the free hand clear of the blade path. Snap off dull segments at the score line (or swap the blade) the moment cutting needs force. Retract the blade before setting the knife down.

title: C-Clamp — Holding Work Tight
body: Place protective pads or scrap wood between the clamp jaws and the workpiece to prevent dents. Tighten until snug plus a quarter turn — over-tightening squeezes all the glue out of a joint. For glue-ups, alternate clamps above and below the board to keep it flat. Position clamps so the work can't pivot out of them. Wipe off glue squeeze-out with a damp cloth before it hardens.
